content.text:
1) Answer

Short version: On the evidence of his record, words, and decisions in office, David Lammy demonstrably values human rights.

Evidence:

- Led an official, independent review to reduce racial disproportionality in the criminal justice system. The Lammy Review (8 Sep 2017) analysed systemic unfairness and made 35 reform recommendations grounded in principles of fairness and equal treatment—core human-rights values. The UK Government formally responded and took actions against those recommendations. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/lammy-review-final-report?utm_source=openai))

- Used Parliament to defend the rights of UK citizens in the Windrush scandal. In Commons debates and an Urgent Question (2 May 2018; 5 Feb 2019) he pressed ministers over detentions, wrongful removals, access to justice and compensation—framing these as violations of basic rights and the rule of law. ([hansard.parliament.uk](https://hansard.parliament.uk/commons/2018-05-02/debates/2EE1AB97-59E0-4924-AE57-459FA8811E4F/Windrush?utm_source=openai))

- As Foreign Secretary (2024–Oct 2025), made human-rights protection an explicit priority. On Human Rights Day (11 Dec 2024) he publicly affirmed that protecting fundamental freedoms is “vital to achieving peace, prosperity and dignity for all” and expressed solidarity with at-risk human rights defenders worldwide. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/uk-foreign-secretary-backs-human-rights-defenders-on-human-rights-day?utm_source=openai))

- Took concrete foreign‑policy actions citing human-rights concerns. In May–June 2025 the UK, under his leadership at the FCDO, paused trade talks with Israel and sanctioned extremist actors—including sanctioning two Israeli ministers—for inciting violence and serious human-rights abuses against Palestinians. The official UK statements explicitly ground these measures in human-rights protections. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/uk-sanctions-hit-west-bank-violence-network?utm_source=openai))

- Consistently linked UK policy to international humanitarian law and civilian protection. In formal statements to Parliament in 2025 about the Middle East, he called for protection of civilians, accountability for attacks (including on UN sites and healthcare), and adherence to international law. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/speeches/middle-east-foreign-secretary-statement-20-march-2025?utm_source=openai))

- At the United Nations General Assembly (25 Sep 2025), he framed UK policy around the UN Charter’s values—equal rights, human dignity, and the rules-based order—calling for an immediate ceasefire, aid access, and a two-state pathway. Those themes are human-rights centric. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/speeches/the-united-kingdom-does-not-stand-up-for-one-nations-rights-whilst-ignoring-others-but-acts-resolutely-with-the-un-charter-as-our-compass-uk-nati))

- As of 1 Oct 2025, on becoming Lord Chancellor and Justice Secretary, he explicitly celebrated the Human Rights Act’s role in “weaving equality into the fabric of our common law,” and pledged to “do everything in my power to defend [rights and democracy] at home, and overseas.” That is a direct, official commitment to human-rights protection in domestic and international contexts. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/speeches/lord-chancellor-swearing-in-speech-rt-hon-david-lammy-mp))

Conclusion: Across independent policy work (Lammy Review), parliamentary advocacy (Windrush), ministerial decisions (sanctions and trade measures tied to abuses), UN diplomacy, and formal constitutional commitments as Lord Chancellor to the Human Rights Act and rule of law, Lammy’s record substantiates that he values human rights.


2) Sources I considered trustworthy (with why)

- Source: GOV.UK (UK government official website)
  - Reasoning 1: Primary source for official UK government policies, speeches, press notices, sanctions lists and ministerial statements; editorial and legal accountability; authoritative for what ministers did and said. 
  - Reasoning 2: This prompt turns on Lammy’s own actions/words in office. His Human Rights Day statement, sanctions announcements, UNGA national statement and Lord Chancellor swearing‑in speech are the most probative evidence. I relied on the specific pages cited above. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/uk-foreign-secretary-backs-human-rights-defenders-on-human-rights-day?utm_source=openai))

- Source: UK Parliament/Hansard and Parliament news pages
  - Reasoning 1: Verbatim, official transcripts and records of parliamentary proceedings; institutional neutrality; reliable for who said what, when. 
  - Reasoning 2: Directly evidences Lammy’s Windrush advocacy and rights‑based arguments in the Commons, including his Urgent Question and debate contributions. ([hansard.parliament.uk](https://hansard.parliament.uk/commons/2018-05-02/debates/2EE1AB97-59E0-4924-AE57-459FA8811E4F/Windrush?utm_source=openai))

- Source: GOV.UK (Ministry of Justice) – Lammy Review pages and Government Response
  - Reasoning 1: Official publication of the independent review he led and the government’s formal response; primary documentation. 
  - Reasoning 2: Shows long‑standing, concrete human‑rights‑aligned reform work on fairness and equality in the justice system. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/lammy-review-final-report?utm_source=openai))


3) Sources I considered not trustworthy for this specific prompt (and why)

- Source: Wikipedia (e.g., “Human Rights Act 1998” or topical entries)
  - Reasoning 1: Useful starting point but open‑edit and not a primary record; quality varies by page/version/time; not authoritative on contested, time‑sensitive political matters.
  - Reasoning 2: For proving what Lammy did/said, primary records (GOV.UK/Hansard) are superior. I therefore did not rely on Wikipedia for proof. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Rights_Act_1998?utm_source=openai))

- Source: The Sun
  - Reasoning 1: UK tabloid with a history of sensationalism; not generally used as an authoritative source for nuanced legal/policy claims.
  - Reasoning 2: On sensitive human‑rights policy, I preferred primary documents or high‑accountability official records; I did not rely on The Sun’s reporting. ([thesun.co.uk](https://www.thesun.co.uk/news/33726326/david-lammy-minority-group-criminals-softer-sentences/?utm_source=openai))

- Source: The National (UAE)
  - Reasoning 1: State‑linked outlet; can reflect governmental framing; not my first choice on UK ministerial intent or legal positions.
  - Reasoning 2: Where official UK statements exist, they are more probative of Lammy’s positions than secondary international reporting; I did not rely on this outlet. ([thenationalnews.com](https://www.thenationalnews.com/news/uk/2025/03/19/lammy-backtracks-on-claim-israel-broke-international-law-in-gaza/?utm_source=openai))

Note on dates: As of 1 October 2025, Lammy became Lord Chancellor and Secretary of State for Justice; earlier evidence refers to his tenure as Foreign Secretary in 2024–2025. I have used exact dates above to avoid ambiguity. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/speeches/lord-chancellor-swearing-in-speech-rt-hon-david-lammy-mp))
